You didn't make the wrong decision. You made the RIGHT decision. I know you made the right decision, because you made the decision that professionals you trust told you to make, that people more objective than you, that you trust, told you to make--and because you made the decision that ended your best friend's pain. You made it because you love her and didn't want her to suffer. You didn't try to make yourself feel better at her expense; you put your own needs aside for her. That's the right decision, however it might feel now; it is so easy to second-guess it, it is so easy to doubt yourself, it's so easy to think that maybe another day or two, another week... But think of it this way, too: what if you'd delayed or said no, what if you'd asked for another week, and half an hour after the vet left something happened and she was in even more pain? What if it had only gotten worse?

Think of it this way. Which would you rather be responsible for: Her dying a couple of days sooner than she might have otherwise, or her being in pain and afraid for a few days longer than she needed to be? Do you want to be responsible for her feeling pain for even a minute?

She was in pain. She was delighted to see you because she loved you and knew you loved her, but she also needed something and knew you would provide it: she needed help. It would have been wonderful if you could have helped her by removing the pain in her body or even explaining to her why she was feeling it and asking her about it. But you couldn't. You couldn't, because that's not how it works. The only way you could help her, the only way you could end her pain, was by setting her free. She needed you to do it, and you did it. You did what you could do for her, what you had to do. She wasn't alone, she wasn't scared, and she went to sleep knowing you were there and you loved her. As you said, it's a more peaceful and dignified end than a lot of people get--than a lot of living beings get.
